content: The Health Guideline Development Group (GDG) was composed of a diverse team of experts in research, guideline development methodologies, clinical policies, and programs aimed at improving outcomes for preterm births. This group also included a representative from the affected population. Based on documents prepared by the Steering Group, the GDG reviewed and interpreted evidence and formulated final recommendations during meetings held from January 27 to February 1, 2022, and March 1 to 3, 2022. They also reviewed and approved the final recommendation document. The World Health Organization (WHO) convened an Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG) consisting of guideline methodologists and systematic review teams. This group was responsible for conducting or updating systematic reviews, appraising evidence, and developing evidence-to-decision frameworks. Technical experts from the Burnet Institute in Australia and the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group (CPC) in the United Kingdom served as guideline methodologists. The CPC provided input on scoping priority questions and supervised the updating of systematic reviews using Cochrane Collaboration standards. The WHO Steering Group coordinated with review authors to conduct a systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) on tocolytic therapy. Evidence was appraised using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. New systematic reviews were commissioned to generate evidence on qualitative and cost-effectiveness studies for other domains of the GRADE evidence-to-decision frameworks. These included reviews of women’s and healthcare professionals’ views and experiences with tocolytic therapy, as well as studies on the cost-effectiveness of tocolytic therapy. The Steering Group worked closely with the ESG to review evidence and prepare GRADE evidence-to-decision frameworks. ESG members attended GDG meetings to provide overviews of synthesized evidence and address technical queries. Representatives from external organizations, including USAID, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), and the International Pediatric Association (IPA), participated in GDG meetings as observers. These organizations, with their history of collaboration with WHO, were identified as key implementers of the recommendations. An external review group, composed of five technical experts with expertise in evidence-based care for improving preterm birth outcomes, reviewed the recommendations. This group was gender-balanced and included members from four WHO regions (Africa, the Americas, South-East Asia, and the Western Pacific). They reviewed the final document for factual accuracy, clarity, contextual issues, and implementation implications. Evidence to support the updated recommendations was derived from multiple sources by systematic review teams in collaboration with the WHO Steering Group. A new systematic review and NMA were commissioned to evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of different classes of tocolytics (e.g., betamimetics, cyclo-oxygenase inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, magnesium sulfate, nitric oxide donors, and combinations of tocolytics) compared to placebo or each other. The review protocol included a clear PICO question, criteria for study identification, search strategies, risk-of-bias assessment methods, and a data analysis plan. The protocol was reviewed and endorsed by the WHO Steering Group and selected ESG members before the systematic review was conducted. Studies were identified through searches of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group’s Trials Register, which includes trials from various databases and journals. Studies from low-, middle-, and high-income countries were considered, with no language restrictions. The systematic review process was iterative, involving constant communication between reviewers, methodologists, and the WHO Steering Group to address challenges and agree on solutions. An additional systematic review update was commissioned to examine the efficacy and safety of tocolytics in specific groups of women to address priority questions not covered by the NMA. Evidence on values, resource use, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility was synthesized through systematic reviews. These reviews included qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods studies on the use of tocolytic therapy to suppress preterm birth. The findings were analyzed using a narrative synthesis approach. Evidence on resource use and cost-effectiveness was based on a systematic review of the literature, synthesizing data from health economic and medical databases. Eligible studies included full economic evaluations assessing cost-benefit, cost-effectiveness, and cost-utility for women receiving tocolytic therapy. The quality of primary studies included in the reviews was assessed using predefined criteria developed by Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth. These criteria addressed research governance, baseline characteristics of participants, population feasibility, and result plausibility. Risk-of-bias assessments followed Cochrane Handbook guidelines, with studies rated as low, high, or unclear risk of bias across various domains. For non-randomized studies, quality assessment was conducted using tools such as ROBINS-I or RoBANS. Mixed-methods studies were appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). The certainty of evidence for effectiveness was rated using the GRADE approach, considering factors such as study design limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Certainty ratings were categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low. For qualitative evidence, the GRADE-CERQual tool was used to assess confidence in findings based on methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance. The GDG formulated recommendations using the GRADE evidence-to-decision framework, which systematically considered evidence on intervention effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. Summary documents for each priority question were prepared, and GDG members reviewed these documents before meetings. During meetings, the GDG collectively reviewed the framework, discussed evidence, and reached consensus on recommendations. The GDG considered the effectiveness of tocolytic agents compared to placebo, the certainty of evidence, and other factors such as cost, acceptability, and feasibility. The GDG classified recommendations into four categories: recommended, not recommended, recommended only in specific contexts, and recommended only in the context of rigorous research. This classification approach has been used for WHO maternal and perinatal health guidelines since 2016. All experts were required to disclose potential conflicts of interest before participating in the guideline development process. The WHO Steering Group reviewed these declarations and determined whether any conflicts were significant enough to affect an expert’s objectivity. Where conflicts were not deemed significant, experts were required to declare them openly at the beginning of GDG meetings. The GDG meetings aimed to discuss evidence and reach consensus on the final wording of recommendations. Consensus was defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of the GDG, provided no strong opposition was expressed. The WHO Steering Group prepared a draft version of the evidence-to-decision framework for participant review before the meetings. Following the meetings, the Steering Group worked with guideline methodologists to finalize the recommendation document, which was then reviewed by GDG members and external independent experts. The GDG issued a main recommendation on tocolytic therapy, consolidating their interpretation of evidence for key priority questions. For example, the GDG identified nifedipine as the preferred tocolytic agent due to its superior balance of benefits, harms, cost, acceptability, and feasibility compared to other agents. Other agents, such as oxytocin receptor antagonists and nitric oxide donors, were noted to prolong pregnancy but were less available and more costly. The GDG also highlighted the risks associated with certain agents, such as betamimetics, and recommended monotherapy over combination therapy.
